rows.title: Planet Money vs. the NBA’s tanking problem
rows.standfirst: What do we want from sports? The very best athletes competing as hard as they know how, putting all their effort and training and natural ability to the test against their opponents. But this time of year, that’s not the product the NBA is putting on the court. Instead, teams at the bottom of the league are competing … to lose, because it could help them get a top pick in next year’s draft. It’s called tanking — it’s bad for fans, and it’s bad for the league.

rows.title: Oil surges to its highest price since 2023, and stocks drop after U.S. jobs report
rows.standfirst: Oil shot to its highest price since 2023 after surging again because of the Iran war, and a weak update on the U.S. job market knocked stocks lower to cap Wall Street's worst week since October.

rows.title: No lawsuits required: U.S. Customs is working on a system to refund tariffs
rows.standfirst: U.S. Customs told the trade court it aims for a streamlined process in 45 days to return importers' money without requiring individual lawsuits.

rows.title: Why are fewer Americans working the night shift?
rows.standfirst: The night shift isn’t for everyone, but it often means a boost in pay and a foot in the door. Yet a smaller share of Americans are working the graveyard shift than in decades past. Today on the show, where did all the third shift workers go?

rows.title: The U.S. unexpectedly loses 92,000 jobs, adding to worries about the economy
rows.standfirst: The job market showed further signs of weakness last month as employers cut 92,000 jobs. The unemployment rate inched up to 4.4%, from 4.3% in January.

rows.title: 2 young billionaires are behind the prediction market boom. They hate each other
rows.standfirst: The 20-something billionaires who run Kalshi and Polymarket are battling it out to be the top prediction market company. Observers and former insiders say the feud is just heating up.

rows.title: Wall Street is betting on tariff refunds after Supreme Court ruling
rows.standfirst: When the Supreme Court struck down many of President Trump's tariffs, it left importers wondering how long they'd have to wait to get their money back. Hedge funds are offering to help out.

rows.title: Want a 2.5% mortgage? Buy it.
rows.standfirst: Remember those juicy mortgage rates from back in 2021? You don’t actually need a time machine to get one today. You just need to find someone willing to sell their house AND their mortgage to you. Called ‘assumable mortgages,’ they take a long time to get, and you’ll probably need a fat wad of cash.

rows.title: WATCH: How traffic dried up in the Strait of Hormuz since the Iran war began
rows.standfirst: The effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz is "about as wrong as things could go" for global oil markets. Iran achieved it not with a naval blockade, but with cheap drones.

rows.title: The Business of Heated Rivalry
rows.standfirst: Heated Rivalry , the steamy hockey romance show, was made for about $2 million per episode. That is remarkably cheap for an hour-long drama.

rows.title: A Biden-era rule sought to stabilize child care. Why Trump wants it gone
rows.standfirst: The Trump administration has proposed repealing a Biden-era rule that required states to change how they pay out child care subsidies, citing the potential for fraud.

rows.title: America has a housing affordability crisis. Building houses for rent can help
rows.standfirst: Developers are building more single-family houses for renting. That can lower prices for both renters and buyers.

rows.title: The anxiety rattling China’s youth
rows.standfirst: China will soon unveil its economic blueprint for the next five years, including a target for economic growth. This comes as consumption is down, wages aren’t rising, and property prices continue to drop. So what’s the plan? Today, we hear from NPR’s China correspondent Jennifer Pak about the challenges facing China’s economic policymakers.FYI, we are going on a book tour! Planet Money’s first ever book comes out in April. We’ll be celebrating in about a dozen cities. There’s a limited edition tote bag included with your ticket, while supplies last. Details, dates and how to get your ticket at planetmoneybook.com. Related episodes:

rows.title: The candy heir vs. chocolate skimpflation
rows.standfirst: The grandson of the Reese's Peanut Butter Cups creator has launched a campaign against The Hershey Company, which owns the Reese's brand. He wants them to stop skimping on ingredients.

rows.title: Why Paramount went looney tunes for Warner Bros.
rows.standfirst: Paramount Skydance is making a $110 billion play for Warner Bros. Discovery, and with it intellectual property like Harry Potter, Batman, and subsidiaries HBO and CNN. On today’s show, who is the man behind the deal? Does he really want to make movies? Will any regulators try to stop it? FYI, we are going on a book tour! Planet Money’s first ever book comes out in April. We’ll be celebrating in about a dozen cities. There’s a limited edition tote bag included with your ticket, while supplies last. Details, dates and how to get your ticket at planetmoneybook.com. Related:

rows.title: Pentagon tightens controls over Stars and Stripes after calling it "woke"
rows.standfirst: The new rules for the independent military newspaper are the Defense Department's latest effort to put extraordinary restrictions on journalists covering the agency.

rows.title: Can you write off a pet dog? How to vet tax advice from social media
rows.standfirst: So you heard a piece of tax advice from a friend or on social media that sounds interesting. Should you try it? A certified public accountant explains how to vet the claim — and avoid getting scammed.

rows.title: Judge blocks DOJ's criminal probe of Federal Reserve, blasting it as political
rows.standfirst: A federal judge has put the brakes on a criminal probe of the Federal Reserve, saying it was part of an improper campaign by the Trump administration to pressure the central bank into cutting interest rates.

rows.title: Chef vs. Robot
rows.standfirst: Robby the chef has lots of endearing qualities. He can make over 5000 dishes, he’s a consistent cook, and he’s never late for work. But he’s not a human. It is a 750 lb. stainless steel robot. With a rotating wok at its center. It’s a wok-bot.

rows.title: Bucking stigma, more places turn to factory-built for affordable housing
rows.standfirst: Mobile homes have long been zoned out of cities and suburbs. But with updated designs and a housing shortage, they're increasingly being welcomed as more-affordable starter homes.

rows.title: Desperate for skilled workers, a furniture maker looks to apprenticeships for relief
rows.standfirst: President Trump has touted apprenticeships as part of his promise of a golden era for American workers. But are his administration's investments enough?

rows.title: Egg prices have taken a beating. What's behind the drop?
rows.standfirst: A year ago, eggs were scarce and prices were sky-high. But avian flu took a much smaller toll on America's egg-laying chickens this winter than last, and egg prices have tumbled 42%.

rows.title: A lot of gas trapped, oil reserves tapped, and Live Nation gets a (tiny) cap
rows.standfirst: It’s Indicators of the Week (now on YouTube!), our weekly look at some of the most fascinating economic numbers from the news.

rows.title: China slams Trump's trade investigation, as it approves a 5-year economic plan
rows.standfirst: China's Foreign Ministry criticized the Trump administration's trade investigation as a "pretext" for tariffs. Meanwhile, China is moving ahead with a five-year plan that may rankle trade partners.

rows.title: Senate passes bipartisan housing bill targeting large investors and easing regulations
rows.standfirst: The 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act would ban large investors from buying up single-family homes.

rows.title: Should colleges accept money from bad people?
rows.standfirst: At a dinner in 2010, physicist Sean Carroll is handed a phone. On the other end: A wealthy patron looking to potentially fund his research. Months later came an invite to a conference. It would take place on an island. The caller was Jeffrey Epstein. Sean declined. Many others didn’t.

rows.title: How the Iran war is disrupting air travel -- and advice if you're planning a trip
rows.standfirst: The war in Iran is roiling jet fuel prices and airlines are beginning to hike prices, unsettling travelers far from the Middle East. If you're booking a flight soon, here are things to know.

rows.title: Countries agree to a historic release of stockpiled oil to ease global disruption
rows.standfirst: Members of the International Energy Agency have announced a coordinated release of 400 million barrels of stockpiled oil in an attempt to counter the disruption in oil trade triggered by the Iran war.

rows.title: 2025 saw relatively fewer natural disasters. Will you get a break on home insurance?
rows.standfirst: Disaster costs fell in the U.S. in 2025. Still, it was the fourth time in five years that extreme weather inflicted more than $100 billion in annual losses. Industry experts say the growing financial toll will make insurers wary of rushing to cut rates.

rows.title: The shadowy world of merchant cash advances
rows.standfirst: During the pandemic, mostly unregulated lenders went after struggling restaurants and music venues, charging at times sky high rates. Now, they’ve found a new market: small businesses that desperately need cash to pay tariffs.

rows.title: Some countries have bet big on EVs
rows.standfirst: Emily Kwong talks with Camila Domonoske, who covers cars and energy for NPR, about how countries and companies that have bet big on electric vehicles are facing new, quickly moving variables in the market and the world.

rows.title: Inside a BOOK auction
rows.standfirst: In the age of TikTok and Polymarket, it can be easy to overlook the humble book. But books are one of the most influential technologies ever invented. From “The Wealth of Nations” to “Das Kapital,” books have the power to shape whole economic systems… and everything else in our world. The market for books can determine which ideas make it to the masses.

rows.title: U.S. judge rules against Pentagon restrictions on press coverage
rows.standfirst: The policy required media organizations to pledge not to gather information unless Defense officials formally authorized its release. A U.S. judge said the rules are at odds with the First Amendment.

rows.title: Jury finds Elon Musk misled investors during Twitter purchase
rows.standfirst: A jury has found Elon Musk liable for misleading investors by deliberately driving down Twitter's stock price in the tumultuous months leading up to his 2022 acquisition of the social media company for $44 billion. But it absolved him of some fraud allegations.

rows.title: CBS News shutters its storied radio news service after nearly a century, ending an era
rows.standfirst: The change is part of a round of layoffs at CBS News. When the radio service began operation in September 1927, it was a precursor to the entire CBS network. Today its top-of-the-hour news roundups are delivered to about 700 stations across the U.S.

rows.title: Why it's so hard for world leaders to bring down oil and gasoline prices
rows.standfirst: From waiving the Jones Act to rerouting oil through the Red Sea, governments are doing their best to make up for the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz, but prices are still rising.

rows.title: Trump and truckers, Poland prospers, and a booming ant biz
rows.standfirst: It’s Indicators of the Week (now on YouTube!). It’s our weekly look at some of the most fascinating economic numbers from the news.

rows.title: FCC approves merger of local television owners Nexstar and Tegna as two lawsuits seek to block it
rows.standfirst: The Federal Communications Commission on Thursday said it had approved the merger of local television giants Nexstar Media Group and rival Tegna, the same day that two lawsuits trying to block the deal were announced.

rows.title: Planned Parenthood chapter settles with EEOC over treatment of white employees
rows.standfirst: The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission says Planned Parenthood of Illinois will pay $500,000 to end an investigation that found the organization's DEI practices violated federal civil rights laws

rows.title: This tax season, there's a new deduction for interest on car loans
rows.standfirst: Taxpayers who purchased a new vehicle in 2025 may qualify for a new deduction on their taxes — even if they're not itemizing. But not everyone is eligible.

rows.title: It's called 'private credit' — and it could lead to big trouble on Wall Street
rows.standfirst: The risky lending business has been booming, but now its problems are becoming increasingly visible on Wall Street and beyond.

rows.title: The Pentagon wants an extra $200 billion for the Iran war and beyond
rows.standfirst: The Trump administration says it is seeking a huge budget to refill and expand its munitions.

rows.title: How Iran is wasting American resources
rows.standfirst: Iran is using an affordable strategy to even the playing field in the war with the U.S. It’s using drones that cost in the thousands of dollars to combat American missiles that cost several million. Military analysts have already signaled concern about the U.S. producing enough munitions, and this isn’t helping. Today on the show, why the U.S. spends so much on munitions and what it’s learning from Iran.

rows.title: Trump temporarily waives the Jones Act to try to lower gasoline prices. Will it work?
rows.standfirst: The Jones Act restricts which ships can carry goods between U.S. ports. Experts say temporarily lifting the act will do little to affect gas prices.

rows.title: The Fed holds interest rates steady as the economy faces deep uncertainty
rows.standfirst: The Federal Reserve held its benchmark interest rate steady as it faces inflationary pressure from the war with Iran — and a weakening labor market.

rows.title: Gas crosses $4 a gallon in the U.S. for the first time in 3 years
rows.standfirst: The war with Iran has driven up gas prices at a time when affordability is high on people's minds.

rows.title: Former Alex Jones employee says: 'It was nonsense, it was lies'
rows.standfirst: Josh Owens spent four years as a video editor and field producer for Jones' Infowars media company. "It was all about making things look cinematic," he says. Owens' memoir is The Madness of Believing.

rows.title: The final batch of World Cup tickets is about to go on sale. Here are 5 things to know
rows.standfirst: FIFA is kicking off its last sales for World Cup tickets on Wednesday. From prices to why FOMO is working against you, here's what you need to know.

rows.title: How Trump's EEOC is attacking DEI and emphasizing white people
rows.standfirst: Andrea Lucas, the Trump-appointed chair of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, has set a new agenda for an agency that long prioritized vulnerable and underserved workers.

rows.title: Who's afraid of private credit?
rows.standfirst: There is a $3 trillion dollar black box at the center of the economy. It’s called private credit. These are direct loans from private investors to private companies. They’re often riskier, less regulated than traditional bank loans – and far less transparent. Spooked investors are scrambling to cash out, and some funds aren’t letting them. It’s all fueling fears of another financial crisis.

rows.title: China's AI chatbots are advanced and versatile — and begging for more users
rows.standfirst: Chinese AI companies are focused less on being cutting edge and more on attracting customers. That means holiday promotions, and making chatbots useful in everyday life.

rows.title: Do school lunches really need an overhaul?
rows.standfirst: School lunch has been revamped a ton over the last two decades. Now, the Trump administration wants to rejigger the menu once more to align with its Make America Healthy Again agenda. That means more meat. More dairy. But do schools really need another menu overhaul? And could they even afford it?

rows.title: Trump says he has 'no problem' with Russian oil tanker bringing relief to Cuba despite blockade
rows.standfirst: President Donald Trump said he has "no problem" with a Russian oil tanker off the coast of Cuba delivering relief to the island, which has been brought to its knees by a U.S. oil blockade.

rows.title: He wants children's bikes made in the U.S.A. — and tariffs against his rivals
rows.standfirst: Nearly all the bicycles sold in the United States are made overseas. An Indiana company set out to change that — and it's seeking a push from the Trump administration's tariffs.

rows.title: Stuck in a long TSA line? Here are some strategies if you need to rebook your flight
rows.standfirst: Extreme TSA lines at airports have left many passengers scrambling to rebook flights missed due to delays. But while airlines say they're helping flyers, they're not obligated to do so.

rows.title: The skyscrapers that NIMBYs and zoning couldn't stop
rows.standfirst: LIVE SHOW TOUR INFO HERE. New stories, live tapings, special guests, book signings and more.

rows.title: How long will the war last? No one knows, and it's making oil prices weird
rows.standfirst: It's like the "Schrödinger's cat" thought experiment. There are two very different potential realities, and traders don't yet know which one is true.

rows.title: The US loses tech hires, sayonora to Sora, and Afroman's win
rows.standfirst: It’s Indicators of the Week (now on YouTube!). It’s our weekly look at some of the most fascinating economic numbers from the news.

rows.title: Judge temporarily blocks Trump administration's Anthropic ban
rows.standfirst: The order briefly stops the government from labeling tech company Anthropic a "supply chain risk," calling that "classic First Amendment retaliation."

rows.title: Trump's attacks on offshore wind could hurt infrastructure spending across the economy
rows.standfirst: President Trump has tried to kill offshore wind's future in the U.S. But industry analysts say the attacks could hurt business confidence across the U.S. economy.
